2.text: Roasted rye-meal is sometimes used in the north as a substitute for tea, but

3.text: it is not much liked by the people. They drink tea in large quantities three

4.text: or four times daily, sometimes as much as forty large cups a day; but it

5.text: does not seem to affect their nervous system. This is due to the fact that

6.text: compressed tea, being prepared of the refuse leaves mixed with sheep or ox

7.text: blood, contains but small quantities of the alkaloid. Europeans travelling in

8.text: that country generally consume nearly as much tea without ill effects. Tea

9.text: is considered by the people as a substitute for food. Its chief importance,

10.text: however, is that it presents an excellent means of restoring heat after travelling

11.text: or walking out of doors in the cold. It is considered to be healthy; and the

12.text: natives believe that in the summer-time, when camping on the damp tundra,

13.text: plenty of hot strong tea keeps off cold and fever. For all these reasons,
13.note: A raised comma-like mark (matching the stress-accent glyph shape used elsewhere on this page, e.g. line 29's Telqäˊp) is printed directly after 'cold', mid-height above the baseline. 'Cold' is plain English, not a Tier-1 form, so the mark cannot be stress notation; per keying_spec.md §2.14 a printer's error is a letter or a word, never a mark of punctuation -- a stray mark is a blot, keyed as nothing. Not keyed.

14.text: scarcity of tea is considered almost everywhere as nothing short of a calamity,

15.text: which, however, befalls the people almost every year for several weeks, when-

16.text: ever the arrival of the merchant caravans is retarded by blizzards or by

18.text: As substitutes for tea, leaves of the sweet-brier, of Epilobium angustifolium

19.text: and of various berries, such as Rubus chamæmorus and Rubus arcticus, are used.
19.note: Species epithet printed with the æ ligature (chamæmorus); machine draft misread it as 'chamgmorus'.

20.text: As stated before, the principal meal of the Chukchee is in the evening,

21.text: after all the people have entered the sleeping-room. At this time the Chuk-

22.text: chee eat much and ravenously. They swallow large quantities of meat, gnaw

23.text: the bones, and try to outdo each other in quickness. Nevertheless the Chuk-

24.text: chee do not seem to be greater eaters than their neighbors; and my cossacks

25.text: and other companions, after a long day spent in travelling through the cold

26.text: weather, ate just as swiftly and ravenously as the natives. There are some

27.text: exceptionally great eaters among the Chukchee, although I myself met such

28.text: a one only among the Russianized Yukaghir of the Kolyma. I was told about

29.text: one Reindeer Chukchee of the Telqäˊp tundra who was able to consume at
29.resolved: Telqäˊp = T,e,l,q,a+U+0308,U+02CA,p -- ä = a + U+0308 COMBINING DIAERESIS; ˊ = U+02CA MODIFIER LETTER ACUTE ACCENT (word stress, keying_spec.md §2.1), postposed to the stressed vowel
29.note: Tier-1 place name (Reindeer Chukchee tundra name). Raised mark after ä read as word stress U+02CA per default (keying_spec.md §4/§5.8), not apostrophe.

30.text: one eating a two-year-old reindeer-buck. I was told that before a meal the

31.text: skin on his stomach lay in large folds, which he gathered up with his belt.

32.text: He could stay without food for two or three days. Then, after a sumptuous

33.text: meal, his stomach would be enormously distended, so that the skin would

34.text: look quite smooth, and he would spend a whole day motionless digesting.

35.text: The Reindeer Chukchee, as well as the Lamut and the Koryak in Kam-

36.text: chatka, occasionally use as food a kind of white clay, which is called nuˊte-
36.resolved: nuˊte- = n,u,U+02CA,t,e,- -- ˊ = U+02CA MODIFIER LETTER ACUTE ACCENT (word stress), postposed to the stressed vowel
36.note: Tier-1 gloss (native word for white clay), hyphenated across lines 36-37: nuˊte-eˊčen. Raised mark read as word stress U+02CA per default.

39.text: Pitch from the larch-tree is used as chewing-gum, as is done by many

40.text: other tribes. For the same purpose the Maritime Chukchee and the Eskimo

41.text: make a preparation of seal-oil by boiling the dregs from the oil till they

42.text: become quite ductile and sticky. A small piece is steeped in fresh seal-oil
